title: Leptospirosis (international guidance)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Suspect after contact with animal urine, floodwater or wet soil in a patient with fever, myalgia and conjunctival suffusion. Start antibiotics on suspicion without waiting for tests: doxycycline for mild disease, IV penicillin or ceftriaxone for severe disease. Early ICU and dialysis for pulmonary haemorrhage and AKI.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Exposure to animal urine or urine-contaminated floodwater, freshwater or wet soil (farming, sewers, flooding, animal work, water sports, adventure travel), usually 5 to 14 days before (range 2 to 30 days).

Abrupt fever, chills, severe headache (sometimes with photophobia), myalgia of the calves and lower back, and conjunctival suffusion; calf and lumbar tenderness with conjunctival suffusion are the most distinguishing signs. Illness may be biphasic.

About 90% have a self-limiting febrile illness; about 10% progress to jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage (especially pulmonary), aseptic meningitis, arrhythmia, respiratory failure or shock. Jaundice with renal failure is Weil disease.
Case fatality is about 5 to 15% in severe illness and can exceed 50% with pulmonary haemorrhage syndrome (CDC). Liver failure is rare despite deep jaundice.

Typical laboratory pattern: thrombocytopenia, neutrophil leucocytosis, high bilirubin with only modestly raised transaminases, raised creatinine, raised creatine kinase and amylase, and an abnormal urine sediment.
Differentials that co-circulate: dengue, malaria, scrub typhus and other rickettsioses, hantavirus, viral hepatitis and bacterial sepsis.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Never delay antibiotics for results: serology is usually negative in the first week and cultures take weeks.
First week: PCR on whole blood and serum (leptospires circulate for about the first 4 to 6 days). After the first week: urine PCR and serology; CSF PCR if meningitic.

IgM ELISA or rapid tests are screening tests. Confirm by MAT with seroconversion or a fourfold rise on a convalescent sample taken 7 to 14 days after the first; single-titre cut-offs (1:100 to 1:800) vary with local endemicity.

Baseline: CBC, creatinine, urea, sodium and potassium, bilirubin and liver enzymes, CK, coagulation, urinalysis, blood gas and lactate, chest X-ray and ECG; test for malaria, dengue and scrub typhus in parallel where endemic.

sections.title: Mild disease (oral)
items: Start as soon as leptospirosis is suspected, ideally before day 5 of illness, but treat whatever the day of presentation (WHO/ILS).
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days is the drug of choice if not contraindicated (CDC).
Alternatives: azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 3 days, amoxicillin 500 mg 6-hourly for 7 days, or ampicillin 500 to 750 mg 6-hourly for 7 days.
Review within 48 to 72 hours, or earlier for falling urine output, jaundice, breathlessness, haemoptysis or bleeding.
Randomised evidence on mortality benefit is of very low certainty (Cochrane 2024), but international guidance still recommends early treatment because it shortens illness and harms are low.

sections.title: Severe disease (IV)
items: Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G) 1.5 million units IV 6-hourly is the drug of choice (CDC); ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily is equally effective. Cefotaxime 1 g IV 6-hourly is a further alternative. Treat for 7 days in total.
Where scrub typhus or other rickettsial infection has not been excluded, add doxycycline (or azithromycin) to the beta-lactam.
Expect a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (fever, rigors, hypotension) within 24 hours of the first dose: give supportive care and continue antibiotics.
Renal impairment: no dose change for ceftriaxone or doxycycline; reduce benzylpenicillin in severe renal failure.

sections.title: Organ support
items: Pulmonary haemorrhage or ARDS: early ICU, early intubation and lung-protective ventilation (tidal volume 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O) with adequate PEEP, and a conservative fluid strategy. Corticosteroids and plasma exchange are unproven.

AKI is often non-oliguric with hypokalaemia: strict fluid and electrolyte balance, replace potassium, and start haemodialysis or haemofiltration (peritoneal dialysis if nothing else) early for oliguria, fluid overload, acidosis or uraemia. Renal function usually recovers.
Shock: crystalloid in small boluses with reassessment, then noradrenaline to a MAP of 65 mmHg; remember Jarisch-Herxheimer and co-existing sepsis.
Bleeding correlates poorly with the platelet count: transfuse for active bleeding and correct coagulopathy rather than treating a number.

sections.title: Escalate to high dependency or ICU
items: Any hypotension, arrhythmia, altered consciousness or active bleeding.
Rising respiratory rate, falling SpO2, haemoptysis (even minor) or new chest X-ray infiltrates; move before respiratory failure is established.
Oliguria, rapidly rising creatinine, hyperkalaemia or acidosis, or jaundice with AKI.

sections.title: Pregnancy, children and national policy
items: Pregnancy: risk of fetal death and miscarriage. Avoid doxycycline; use amoxicillin, ampicillin or azithromycin for mild disease and IV penicillin or ceftriaxone for severe disease, with obstetric input.
Children (if seen): doxycycline 2 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (maximum 200 mg/day) for 7 days (CDC).
Late sequelae include uveitis weeks to months later, and prolonged fatigue or mood change; arrange review for new eye symptoms.
India: NCDC uses benzylpenicillin 2 million units 6-hourly and weekly doxycycline chemoprophylaxis for high-risk workers in season; this protocol follows WHO/ILS and CDC.

sections.title: Prevention
items: Protective footwear, gloves and clothing for high-risk work; avoid wading, swimming or immersing the head in floodwater or freshwater; cover cuts and abrasions; rodent control.

Chemoprophylaxis (CDC): doxycycline 200 mg orally once weekly, starting 1 to 2 days before and continuing through short-term high-risk exposure. Evidence of benefit is limited and nausea is common (Cochrane).
After a known high-risk exposure such as a laboratory accident, WHO/ILS advises a full treatment course.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Waiting for MAT or ELISA before starting antibiotics.
Labelling fever with jaundice as viral hepatitis without checking creatinine, CK and urine.
Underestimating mild haemoptysis or tachypnoea, which can precede fatal pulmonary haemorrhage.
Missing co-infection with dengue, malaria or scrub typhus.

drugs.name: Doxycycline
drugs.dose: 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days (children 2 mg/kg/day in 2 doses, maximum 200 mg/day)
drugs.notes: Mild disease, drug of choice. Avoid in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Azithromycin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally once daily for 3 days

drugs.name: Amoxicillin
drugs.dose: 500 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days

drugs.name: Ampicillin
drugs.dose: 500 to 750 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days

drugs.name: Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G)
drugs.dose: 1.5 million units IV every 6 hours for 7 days
drugs.notes: Severe disease, drug of choice (CDC). Watch for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Reduce in severe renal failure.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.dose: 1 g IV once daily for 7 days
drugs.notes: Severe disease; as effective as penicillin.

drugs.name: Cefotaxime
drugs.dose: 1 g IV every 6 hours for 7 days

drugs.name: Doxycycline chemoprophylaxis
drugs.notes: Start 1 to 2 days before and continue through short-term high-risk exposure.
